title: Population collapse in the Americas after 1492
summary: A 2019 study estimates about 60.5 million people lived in the Americas before 1492, and that European epidemics removed 90% of them over the next century. Diseases included smallpox, measles and mumps. Its authors estimate that 55.8 million hectares of abandoned land regrew, drawing down carbon and helping lower atmospheric CO2 by 3.5 ppm, part of a global decline in the late 1500s and early 1600s.

uncertainty.note: Begins with European arrival in 1492; high-mortality epidemics and depopulation continued through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

where.modern_name: The Americas; stand-in pin at Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic
where.historical_name: Hispaniola, Caribbean (initial point of European epidemiological contact in the Americas)

importance.justification: Catastrophic depopulation of the Americas destroyed indigenous civilizations, enabled trans-Atlantic European colonization, and altered global atmospheric carbon levels.

audience_note: Describes catastrophic loss of human life and societal collapse caused by introduced epidemic diseases and colonial violence.

related.because: Columbus's 1492 voyage established permanent transatlantic contact, directly introducing Old World pathogens into immunologically naive American populations.

sources.title: Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492 (Quaternary Science Reviews 207:13–36)
sources.publisher: White Rose Research Online (Universities of Leeds, Sheffield & York)
sources.author: Alexander Koch, Chris Brierley, Mark M. Maslin, Simon L. Lewis

sources.title: U.S. History: 2.4 New Worlds in the Americas: Labor, Commerce, and the Columbian Exchange
sources.author: P. Scott Corbett et al.

reviewer_note: The figures are estimates with wide ranges, for example 44.8 to 78.2 million people. Violence and forced labour also played a part but are not measured here. The pin is a stand-in for two continents.
